Section 8.1 — The Biblical Design for Sex and Marriage

We must begin where Scripture begins, with a good gift and not a prohibition, because the church has too often let the world cast it as the enemy of sex when in fact the church is its truest friend. God made human beings male and female, and He made sexual union, and He pronounced His creation very good before sin ever entered. Sex is not a regrettable necessity or a shameful thing the Bible reluctantly tolerates. It is the deliberate design of a wise and generous God, who gave it to husband and wife as a gift of union, delight, and the bringing forth of life. "Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled" (Hebrews 13:4). Honorable. Undefiled. Let no preacher leave his people thinking God is embarrassed by what God Himself created.

But the goodness of the gift is inseparable from the design of the Giver, and here the world and the Word part ways. From the beginning, sexual union was ordered to one place and one place only: the covenant of marriage between a man and a woman. "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). The one-flesh union is covenantal, not casual; it is the bodily seal of a lifelong promise, not a recreation to be enjoyed wherever desire leads. This is why Scripture calls for chastity outside of marriage and fidelity within it — not because it thinks little of sex, but because it thinks so much of it. You honor a fire by keeping it in the hearth, where it warms the house; loosed from the hearth, the same fire burns the house down. The Christian sexual ethic is not the suppression of a good thing but the protection of it.

This vision of the male-and-female, one-flesh covenant rests on the design we studied in Unit 4, and it is the standard against which every question in this unit will be measured. Teach it positively. A people who have seen the beauty of God's design will be far better armed against its counterfeits than a people who have only ever heard what is forbidden.
Section 8.2 — Pornography: Its Destructiveness and the Path to Freedom

Of all the sexual sins now besieging the church, none is more widespread or more quietly devastating than pornography, and the pastor who imagines his congregation untouched by it is dreaming. It reaches into Christian homes, into the lives of officeholders, and, let us be honest, into the studies of pastors themselves. We must speak of it plainly and without panic, as physicians speak of a disease they intend to treat.

Understand first why it is so destructive. Pornography takes human beings made in the image of God and trains the heart to consume them as objects for one's own use — the very opposite of love, which gives itself for the good of another. It is, by our Lord's own definition, a form of adultery committed in the heart: "whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). And it does not stay still. It follows the pattern of every enslaving sin, demanding more to deliver less, isolating its captive, corroding his capacity for real intimacy, and feeding always on secrecy — for as we learned in earlier units, sin grows strong in the dark and withers in the light.

Which points directly to the path of freedom, and there is a real path; no one need despair. The first step is confession that drags the thing into the light: "Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed" (James 5:16). The secret sin thrives in darkness and isolation; once spoken aloud to a trusted brother, its power to control through shame and secrecy is broken, even though the underlying struggle itself is not instantly resolved. Then comes honest accountability — not a one-time confession but an ongoing openness to men permitted to ask the hard questions. And undergirding it all must be the gospel, for here above all a man must remember the lesson of Unit 2: holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, not the achievement of gritted teeth. Willpower alone has never broken an enslaving sin and never will; what breaks it is the grace of God working in a soul that has stopped fighting alone. The pastor's task is to address this sin in his flock without ever winking at it as harmless or crushing the struggler as hopeless — to call men to repentance and to walk patiently beside them in it, knowing that freedom in Christ is real and that many who now stand free once thought they never could.
Section 8.3 — Pastoral Wisdom in Contested Cultural Questions

Some of the questions raised in this unit have become denominational and cultural flashpoints. This course does not require students to adopt a CTS position on those disputed questions. Pastors should study the relevant biblical texts carefully, understand how faithful Christians and their church traditions interpret them, and teach within their ministry setting with theological integrity, humility, and pastoral care.

Whatever conclusion a pastor or church reaches, every person must be treated as one who bears the image of God. Controversy never gives Christians permission for contempt, cruelty, caricature, or careless speech. Pastoral ministry deals with people rather than abstractions, and difficult questions should therefore be approached with patience, careful listening, truthfulness, and compassion.

A pastor must guard against treating any single sin as though it sat in a class by itself, more disqualifying than the sins a congregation tolerates comfortably in itself. The very word Scripture most often uses for sin, hamartia, means simply to miss the mark — and Scripture's own lists of sin are strikingly plural, never built around one offense alone. Our Lord Himself gave such a list: "For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lewdness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within and defile a man" (Mark 7:21-23, NKJV). Thirteen things named in one breath, with no ranking among them — pride and foolishness standing beside murder and adultery. A pastor who has read that list carefully will be slow to build his preaching, or his congregation's sense of shame, around any single item drawn out and elevated above the rest.

History offers a case in point, and Scripture is not silent on it. God's own verdict on divorce is plain: "For the LORD God of Israel says That He hates divorce, for it covers one's garment with violence," says the LORD of hosts (Malachi 2:16, NKJV). And Christ Himself named the sin directly: "whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery" (Matthew 19:9, NKJV). This is not a minor matter softened by time; it is a sin God says He hates, and one Christ calls by its full name. Yet a generation or two ago, many congregations treated divorce as very nearly the unpardonable sin, and a divorced believer often carried a weight of shame the rest of the church never had to carry for its own besetting faults. Today, with a large share of any congregation having experienced divorce and remarriage, that same sin — real, named, and taken seriously by God Himself — is rarely singled out that way at all, and divorced and remarried believers sit in the pew forgiven, restored, and serving alongside everyone else. If a sin God hates and Christ names adultery can be received into the ordinary, forgiven life of the church without being held over anyone forever, no pastor has grounds to treat some other struggle as though it stood outside that same grace.

Scripture also distinguishes, as it does with every temptation, between an attraction and an act. To be tempted is not the same as to sin; every believer, whatever the particular shape of his own temptations, wages the same war against desires he did not choose and does not fully control (James 1:14-15). Whatever chastity or repentance a pastor calls a congregant to, he is calling him to nothing stranger or harder than what he asks of every believer in the church — the same call to hold every desire under Christ that every saint, whatever his own struggle, is asked to carry.

No person's past, and no person's present struggle, places him beyond grace. The gospel that changed the church's comfortable sins can change any sin, and a pastor who has watched an entire congregation's attitude toward one sin soften over a generation should be slow to declare any other sin the permanent exception.

CTS distinguishes between doctrines central to the gospel and secondary or disputed questions on which evangelical churches may draw their boundaries differently. Students should learn to explain their own convictions from Scripture without pretending that every Christian who interprets a difficult passage differently has abandoned biblical authority. The church is called to hold the truth it believes with the posture of a hospital, not a battlefield — treating every person who walks through its doors, whatever he is carrying, as someone Christ died to heal, not an enemy to be defeated. The goal here is not to settle a denominational controversy for the student, but to form pastors who can handle controversial questions biblically, accurately, and graciously.
Section 8.4 — Truth-Telling with Compassion in the Local Church

All of this comes to rest, finally, not in a position paper but in a pastoral practice carried out in the local church, for that is where sexual discipleship actually happens or fails to happen. And make no mistake: every person in your congregation is being discipled in his sexuality by something. If the church is silent, the culture will not be; it catechizes relentlessly, through every screen and song, and a people left untaught by their pastor will simply be taught by the world instead. Silence is not neutrality. The pastor who will not speak of these things has not avoided forming his people's sexual ethic; he has merely surrendered the forming of it to other hands.

So teach — and teach positively, not only prohibitively. A congregation that hears only the list of forbidden things will conclude that Christianity is against sex, and will be defenseless when the world offers what looks like a more generous vision. But a congregation that has been shown the beauty and meaning of God's design — sex as covenant, the body as the Lord's, marriage as a picture of Christ and the church, singleness as an honorable and fruitful calling — has been given something worth living for, and the prohibitions then make sense as the fence around a garden rather than the bars of a cage.

Through all of it, hold the posture this course has pressed again and again: never truth without love, and never a love that abandons truth. The two are not in tension; they meet perfectly in Christ, who was full of grace and truth, and who neither lowered the standard for the woman caught in sin nor crushed her beneath it. Let your church be a community where strugglers of every kind — and that is all of us — find at once the clear call to holiness and the abundant means of grace and honest friendship to pursue it. No one who walks through your doors is beyond the reach of the gospel, and there is no sexual sin the blood of Christ cannot cleanse and no sexual brokenness His grace cannot, in time, redeem. Preach that, and live as though you believe it, and you will be the kind of shepherd these wounded and confused generations most desperately need.

sa.prompt: 21. Why does the unit insist the church begin its teaching on sex with a good gift, not a prohibition?
sa.model: The church must begin its teaching on sex with a good gift and not a prohibition, because Scripture does. Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage and the marriage bed honorable and undefiled, and Genesis 2:24 describes the man and wife becoming one flesh within the covenant. The Christian sexual ethic is not the suppression of a good thing but the protection of it—like a fire honored by being kept in the hearth. Pastors should teach the design positively, so people see its beauty, not only its fences.

es_reference.prompt: 21. ¿Por qué insiste la unidad en que la iglesia comience su enseñanza sobre el sexo con un buen don, no una prohibición?
es_reference.model: La iglesia debe comenzar su enseñanza sobre el sexo con un buen don y no una prohibición, porque la Escritura lo hace. Hebreos 13:4 llama al matrimonio y al lecho matrimonial honroso y sin mancilla, y Génesis 2:24 describe al hombre y la esposa convirtiéndose en una sola carne dentro del pacto. La ética sexual cristiana no es la supresión de algo bueno sino la protección de ello — como un fuego honrado al mantenerse en el hogar. Los pastores deben enseñar el diseño positivamente, para que la gente vea su belleza, no solo sus cercas.

sa.prompt: 22. Explain why pornography is destructive and what Matthew 5:28 says about lust.
sa.model: Pornography is destructive because it trains the heart to consume image-bearers as objects rather than to love sacrificially. By Christ's own definition in Matthew 5:28, lustful looking is adultery committed in the heart, so it is no harmless private matter. Like every enslaving sin it feeds always on secrecy, growing in the dark. It corrodes the very capacity for the self-giving love that marriage requires.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Explique por qué la pornografía es destructiva y qué dice Mateo 5:28 sobre la codicia.
es_reference.model: La pornografía es destructiva porque entrena al corazón a consumir a los portadores de imagen como objetos en vez de amar sacrificialmente. Por la definición misma de Cristo en Mateo 5:28, el mirar con codicia es adulterio cometido en el corazón, de modo que no es un asunto privado inofensivo. Como todo pecado esclavizante se alimenta siempre del secreto, creciendo en la oscuridad. Corroe la capacidad misma para el amor que se entrega que el matrimonio requiere.

sa.prompt: 23. Describe the path to freedom from an enslaving sexual sin.
sa.model: The first step is confession that drags the thing into the light, since the sin feeds on secrecy; James 5:16 says to confess to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. Beyond a one-time confession, freedom requires ongoing honest accountability. And what finally breaks an enslaving sin is not sheer willpower but the grace of God in a soul no longer fighting alone. The pastor addresses such sin without winking at it or crushing the struggler as hopeless.

es_reference.prompt: 23. Describa el camino a la libertad de un pecado sexual esclavizante.
es_reference.model: El primer paso es la confesión que arrastra la cosa a la luz, pues el pecado se alimenta del secreto; Santiago 5:16 dice confesar unos a otros y orar los unos por los otros, para que sean sanados. Más allá de una confesión de una sola vez, la libertad requiere una rendición de cuentas honesta continua. Y lo que finalmente quiebra un pecado esclavizante no es la pura fuerza de voluntad sino la gracia de Dios en un alma que ya no pelea sola. El pastor trata tal pecado sin guiñarle el ojo ni aplastar al que lucha como sin esperanza.

sa.prompt: 24. How should a pastor approach a cultural question on which evangelical churches disagree?
sa.model: The pastor should study the relevant biblical texts carefully, understand his church's convictions and the strongest arguments of Christians who disagree, and minister with theological integrity, humility, careful listening, truthfulness, and compassion. CTS does not settle every secondary controversy for the student.

es_reference.prompt: 24. ¿Cómo debe abordar un pastor una cuestión cultural sobre la cual discrepan las iglesias evangélicas?
es_reference.model: El pastor debe estudiar cuidadosamente los textos bíblicos pertinentes, comprender las convicciones de su iglesia y los argumentos más fuertes de los cristianos que discrepan, y ministrar con integridad teológica, humildad, escucha cuidadosa, veracidad y compasión. CTS no resuelve por el estudiante toda controversia secundaria.

And if a sin God hates can be received into the ordinary, forgiven life of the church without being held over anyone forever, no pastor has grounds to treat another struggle as outside that same grace.

es_reference.prompt: 25. Explique la lección pastoral del ejemplo histórico del divorcio, y cómo debería moldear qué pecados enfatiza un pastor.
es_reference.model: Hace una generación o dos, muchas congregaciones trataban el divorcio casi como el pecado imperdonable, y el creyente divorciado a menudo cargaba un peso de vergüenza que el resto de la iglesia nunca tuvo que cargar por sus propias faltas habituales. Sin embargo, el divorcio es un pecado que Dios aborrece (Malaquías 2:16) y que Cristo llama adulterio (Mateo 19:9). Hoy, con una gran parte de cualquier congregación habiendo vivido el divorcio y las segundas nupcias, ese mismo pecado, real, nombrado y tomado en serio por Dios mismo, rara vez se señala de ese modo, y los creyentes divorciados y vueltos a casar se sientan en la banca perdonados, restaurados y sirviendo. La lección para el pastor es doble. Debe ser lento para construir su predicación, o el sentido de vergüenza de su congregación, en torno a un solo pecado elevado sobre los demás: las listas de pecados de la propia Escritura, como Marcos 7:21-23 con trece cosas nombradas de un solo aliento, son plurales y sin jerarquía, con el orgullo y la insensatez junto al homicidio y al adulterio. Y si un pecado que Dios aborrece puede ser recibido en la vida ordinaria y perdonada de la iglesia sin que se le reproche a nadie para siempre, ningún pastor tiene base para tratar otra lucha como si estuviera fuera de esa misma gracia.

sa.prompt: 26. Why must the church speak about sexuality rather than stay silent?
sa.model: If the church is silent about sexuality, the culture will catechize relentlessly in its place. A congregation that hears only the list of forbidden things will conclude that Christianity is merely against sex. But shown the beauty of God's design, the same congregation will see the prohibitions as the fence around a garden rather than the bars of a cage. Sexual discipleship happens, or fails, in the local church, so the church must speak.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Por qué debe la iglesia hablar sobre la sexualidad en vez de callar?
es_reference.model: Si la iglesia calla sobre la sexualidad, la cultura catequizará sin descanso en su lugar. Una congregación que oye solo la lista de las cosas prohibidas concluirá que el cristianismo está meramente contra el sexo. Pero mostrada la belleza del diseño de Dios, la misma congregación verá las prohibiciones como la cerca alrededor de un jardín en vez de los barrotes de una jaula. El discipulado sexual sucede, o fracasa, en la iglesia local, así que la iglesia debe hablar.

sa.prompt: 27. Summarize the posture 'never truth without love' as the unit applies it to sexuality.
sa.model: The posture pressed throughout the course is never truth without love, and never a love that abandons truth. The unit points to Christ, who with the woman caught in sin neither lowered the standard nor crushed her beneath it. The pastor is to do the same: holding the biblical design without flinching, while extending the grace that lifts rather than condemns. Truth and love are not rivals but partners in every hard conversation.

es_reference.prompt: 27. Resuma la postura «nunca la verdad sin amor» tal como la unidad la aplica a la sexualidad.
es_reference.model: La postura urgida a lo largo del curso es nunca la verdad sin amor, y nunca un amor que abandona la verdad. La unidad señala a Cristo, que con la mujer sorprendida en pecado ni bajó la norma ni la aplastó bajo ella. El pastor ha de hacer lo mismo: sosteniendo el diseño bíblico sin pestañear, mientras extiende la gracia que levanta en vez de condenar. La verdad y el amor no son rivales sino compañeros en cada conversación difícil.

sa.prompt: 28. What is the unit's closing assurance about sexual sin and the gospel?
sa.model: The unit's closing assurance is that no one who walks through the church's doors is beyond the reach of the gospel: there is no sexual sin the blood of Christ cannot cleanse, and no sexual brokenness His grace cannot, in time, redeem. This holds out real hope to the struggler and the fallen alike, since freedom in Christ is real and many who now stand free once thought they never could. The pastor is to preach that and live as though he believes it.

es_reference.prompt: 28. ¿Cuál es la seguridad final de la unidad sobre el pecado sexual y el evangelio?
es_reference.model: El cierre de la unidad asegura que nadie que cruce las puertas de la iglesia está fuera del alcance del evangelio: no hay pecado sexual que la sangre de Cristo no pueda limpiar, ni quebranto sexual que Su gracia no pueda, con el tiempo, redimir. Esto ofrece verdadera esperanza al que lucha y al caído por igual, pues la libertad en Cristo es real y muchos que hoy están libres creyeron alguna vez que nunca podrían. El pastor ha de predicar eso y vivir como si lo creyera.

sa.prompt: 29. How should a pastor address sexual sin without either winking at it or crushing the struggler?
sa.model: The pastor's task is to address the sin honestly, neither winking at it as though it did not matter nor crushing the struggler as hopeless. He names the sin as sin, dragging it out of the secrecy it feeds on, while holding out the grace of God to a soul no longer fighting alone. Honest accountability and gentle perseverance, not condemnation, mark the path. The aim is always to lift the fallen toward freedom, not to grind him down.

es_reference.prompt: 29. ¿Cómo debe un pastor tratar el pecado sexual sin guiñarle el ojo ni aplastar al que lucha?
es_reference.model: La tarea del pastor es tratar el pecado honestamente, ni guiñándole el ojo como si no importara ni aplastando al que lucha como sin esperanza. Nombra el pecado como pecado, arrastrándolo fuera del secreto del que se alimenta, mientras extiende la gracia de Dios a un alma que ya no pelea sola. La rendición de cuentas honesta y la perseverancia suave, no la condenación, marcan el camino. La meta es siempre levantar al caído hacia la libertad, no molerlo.

sa.prompt: 30. Why does the unit treat the beauty of God's design as essential to teaching sexual ethics?
sa.model: If the church teaches only prohibitions, people conclude Christianity is against sex and the culture's louder catechesis wins by default. Shown the beauty of God's design—a good gift, one flesh, a fire honored in its place—a congregation sees the prohibitions as the fence around a garden rather than the bars of a cage. Teaching the design positively protects the gift and makes the boundaries intelligible. Beauty, not bare rule-keeping, is what finally persuades the heart.

es_reference.prompt: 30. ¿Por qué trata la unidad la belleza del diseño de Dios como esencial para enseñar la ética sexual?
es_reference.model: Si la iglesia enseña solo prohibiciones, la gente concluye que el cristianismo está contra el sexo y la más ruidosa catequesis de la cultura gana por defecto. Mostrada la belleza del diseño de Dios — un buen don, una sola carne, un fuego honrado en su lugar — una congregación ve las prohibiciones como la cerca alrededor de un jardín en vez de los barrotes de una jaula. Enseñar el diseño positivamente protege el don y hace inteligibles los límites. La belleza, no el mero cumplir reglas, es lo que finalmente persuade al corazón.

title: Unit 8 - Sexual Ethics, Purity, and Gender
